title: Capacity planning
description: Learn about Capacity planning. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: **Capacity planning** ensures your system can handle growth without performance degradation. This lesson teaches you to model traffic, size infrastructure, and scale proactively instead of reactively.
What Is Capacity Planning

Capacity planning is the process of determining the infrastructure resources needed to meet current and future demand. It involves modeling traffic growth, measuring resource utilization, and provisioning capacity before bottlenecks occur. Reactive capacity management means adding resources after users complain. Proactive capacity planning means adding resources before users notice.

terms.definition: The process of determining the infrastructure resources needed to meet current and future demand.
The buffer between current utilization and maximum capacity, typically 20 to 30 percent.
The resource that limits system throughput, such as CPU, memory, disk I/O, or network.
The degree to which a resource is utilized relative to its maximum capacity.
The ability of a system to handle increased load by adding resources.

data.title: Senior Engineer Mindset
data.text: Capacity planning is not an infrastructure team problem. It is an engineering problem. Every engineer should understand how their service consumes resources and how to size it for growth.
Capacity Planning Process

A robust capacity planning process has five steps: measure current utilization, model growth, identify bottlenecks, provision capacity, and monitor results. Run the process quarterly for core services and before every major launch. Document the assumptions and share the plan with stakeholders.

items: Measure current utilization of CPU, memory, disk, and network
Model traffic growth based on historical trends and business plans
Identify bottlenecks using utilization metrics and profiling
Provision capacity with 20 to 30 percent headroom
Monitor results and adjust the model quarterly

data.text: Measuring Utilization

Capacity planning depends on accurate utilization measurements. Use monitoring tools such as Prometheus, Datadog, or CloudWatch to collect CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network metrics. Measure peak utilization, not average. A service that averages 50 percent CPU but peaks at 90 percent during traffic spikes needs more capacity than the average suggests.

items: Use percentiles (p95, p99) for latency and resource metrics
Separate user-facing peaks from batch processing spikes

data.text: Traffic Growth Modeling

Traffic growth can be modeled using historical data and business projections. Linear growth assumes a constant increase in traffic. Exponential growth assumes a compounding increase, common in viral products. Step growth assumes sudden jumps due to marketing campaigns or new features. Use the model that best fits your business and update it quarterly.

rows: Products with seasonal or campaign-driven traffic

data.text: Identifying Bottlenecks

A bottleneck is the resource that limits system throughput. Use profiling tools such as flame graphs, heap dumps, and iostat to identify the bottleneck. CPU saturation means the service needs more compute or better algorithms. Memory saturation means the service needs more RAM or better memory management. Disk I/O saturation means the service needs faster storage or better caching.

items: CPU saturation: optimize algorithms or add compute
Memory saturation: optimize memory usage or add RAM
Disk I/O saturation: add caching or faster storage
Network saturation: add bandwidth or reduce payload size

data.text: Provisioning with Headroom

Provision capacity with 20 to 30 percent headroom above projected peak. Headroom absorbs traffic spikes, unexpected growth, and failed instances. If your peak utilization is 1000 RPS, provision for 1200 to 1300 RPS. Without headroom, a small traffic spike saturates the system and triggers an incident.

data.title: Headroom Calculation
data.text: Provision at 120 to 130 percent of projected peak. Running at 100 percent leaves no room for spikes and will cause incidents.
Auto-Scaling

Auto-scaling adjusts capacity automatically based on demand. Horizontal pod autoscaler in Kubernetes scales the number of pods based on CPU or custom metrics. AWS Auto Scaling adjusts EC2 instances based on CloudWatch alarms. Configure auto-scaling with appropriate thresholds and cooldown periods to avoid flapping.

items: Set scale-up threshold at 70 percent CPU for 5 minutes
Set scale-down threshold at 40 percent CPU for 15 minutes
Configure cooldown periods to prevent flapping
Set minimum and maximum instance counts

data.text: Capacity Planning for Databases

Database capacity planning requires forecasting storage, IOPS, and connection pool usage. Measure current storage growth rate and project when the disk will be full. Measure current IOPS and compare to the database maximum. Measure connection pool utilization and compare to the configured maximum. Provision capacity before any of these limits is reached.

data.title: Database Capacity Forecast
data.content: Forecast when the database will reach capacity limits based on current growth rates.
data.code:
current_storage_gb = 500
growth_per_month_gb = 50
max_storage_gb = 2000
months_to_full = (max_storage_gb - current_storage_gb) / growth_per_month_gb
print(f"Months to full: {months_to_full:.1f}")
# Months to full: 30.0

current_iops = 8000
max_iops = 10000
growth_per_month_iops = 500
months_to_io_limit = (max_iops - current_iops) / growth_per_month_iops
print(f"Months to IO limit: {months_to_io_limit:.1f}")
# Months to IO limit: 4.0

data.text: Capacity Planning for Caches

Caches such as Redis or Memcached need capacity planning for memory, eviction rate, and network bandwidth. Monitor the hit rate: if it drops below 95 percent, the cache is too small. Monitor the eviction rate: if keys are being evicted before TTL, increase memory. Monitor network bandwidth: if the cache is saturating the network, add cache nodes or use a faster network.

items: Monitor cache hit rate; target above 95 percent
Monitor eviction rate; increase memory if evictions are high
Monitor network bandwidth; add nodes if saturated
Plan for 30 percent growth in key count

data.text: Capacity Planning for Message Queues

Message queues need capacity planning for storage, throughput, and consumer lag. Monitor queue depth: if it exceeds 100,000 messages, the consumers cannot keep up. Monitor throughput: if messages per second exceeds the consumer group capacity, add consumers. Monitor storage: if disk usage exceeds 80 percent, add storage or reduce retention.

data.title: Queue Capacity
data.text: A growing queue indicates that consumers are falling behind. Add consumers or optimize consumer processing before the queue saturates.
Capacity Planning for CDNs

CDN capacity planning involves bandwidth, cache hit ratio, and origin load. Monitor the cache hit ratio: if it drops below 90 percent, review caching rules. Monitor bandwidth: if the CDN is approaching its bandwidth limit, upgrade the plan or add a second CDN. Monitor origin load: if origin requests increase, the cache is not working effectively.

items: Target cache hit ratio above 90 percent
Monitor bandwidth and upgrade before limits
Monitor origin load and optimize caching rules
Plan for 2x bandwidth growth during marketing campaigns

data.text: Capacity Planning for Serverless

Serverless capacity planning is different because the platform manages infrastructure. Your job is to configure concurrency limits, provisioned concurrency, and regional limits. Monitor cold start latency: if it exceeds 500 milliseconds, increase provisioned concurrency. Monitor throttles: if the function is being throttled, request a limit increase from the cloud provider.

items: Set concurrency limits based on peak traffic projections
Use provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive functions
Monitor throttles and request limit increases proactively

data.text: Capacity Planning and Load Testing

Load testing validates capacity plans by simulating production traffic. Run load tests in staging with production-like data and traffic patterns. Ramp up traffic gradually to find the breaking point. The breaking point is the maximum throughput before latency or errors exceed the SLO. Capacity should be sized at 120 to 130 percent of the breaking point.

data.title: Load Testing
data.text: Run load tests quarterly and before every major launch. Ramp up traffic gradually and record the breaking point. Size capacity at 120 to 130 percent of the breaking point.
Capacity Planning and Cost Optimization

Capacity planning and cost optimization are intertwined. Over-provisioning wastes money. Under-provisioning causes incidents. Use reserved instances for baseline capacity and on-demand for spikes. Use auto-scaling to match capacity with demand. Right-size instances based on utilization data. The goal is to meet the SLO at the lowest cost.
Capacity Planning and SLOs

SLOs and capacity planning are closely linked. When capacity is insufficient, the SLO suffers. Monitor the error budget alongside capacity metrics. If utilization exceeds 70 percent, trigger a capacity review. If utilization exceeds 90 percent, page the on-call engineer. Use error budget exhaustion as a signal to scale.

items: Set a capacity SLO at 70 percent peak utilization
Alert when utilization exceeds 70 percent for 10 minutes
Review capacity quarterly based on traffic growth
Provision 30 percent headroom above projected peak

data.text: Capacity Planning and Multi-Region

Multi-region capacity planning requires distributing traffic and capacity across regions. Monitor per-region utilization and shift traffic if one region approaches capacity. Use DNS-based geo-routing or global load balancers. Plan for region failover: if one region fails, the other regions must absorb the traffic.

items: Shift traffic if a region exceeds 70 percent utilization
Plan for failover capacity in each region

data.text: Capacity Planning and Seasonal Traffic

Seasonal traffic patterns such as Black Friday, holiday shopping, or tax season require special capacity planning. Model the seasonal spike using historical data. Provision additional capacity two weeks before the event. Scale down after the event to save cost. Use auto-scaling with pre-warming to handle the spike without manual intervention.

data.title: Seasonal Capacity
data.text: Use historical data to model seasonal spikes. Provision two weeks before the event and scale down two weeks after.
Capacity Planning and Marketing Campaigns

Marketing campaigns can cause sudden traffic spikes. Work with the marketing team to get the campaign calendar. Model the expected traffic increase and provision capacity accordingly. Pre-warm auto-scaling groups before the campaign launch. Monitor traffic in real time and be ready to scale manually if the spike exceeds projections.

items: Monitor traffic in real time during the campaign

data.text: Capacity Planning and Data Growth

Data growth affects storage, backup, and processing capacity. Monitor database storage growth rate and project when the disk will be full. Monitor backup size and retention requirements. Monitor data pipeline processing time and throughput. Provision storage and compute capacity before limits are reached.

items: Project when storage will reach limits

data.text: Capacity Planning and Logging

Logging infrastructure needs capacity planning for ingestion, storage, and query performance. Monitor log ingestion rate and compare to the logging platform limit. Monitor storage usage and retention requirements. Monitor query performance and index size. Provision capacity before any of these limits is reached.

data.title: Logging Capacity Forecast
data.content: Forecast when the logging platform will reach capacity limits based on current growth rates.
data.code:
current_logs_per_day_gb = 100
growth_per_month = 0.15  # 15%
max_storage_gb = 2000
retention_months = 12

# Current total stored logs
current_stored = current_logs_per_day_gb * 30 * retention_months
months_to_full = 0
stored = current_stored
while stored < max_storage_gb:
    stored *= (1 + growth_per_month)
    months_to_full += 1

print(f"Months to full: {months_to_full}")
# Months to full: 18

data.text: Capacity Planning and CI/CD

CI/CD pipelines need capacity planning for build agents, artifact storage, and test execution. Monitor build queue length and agent utilization. If builds are queuing for more than 10 minutes, add agents. Monitor artifact storage and retention. If storage exceeds 80 percent, add storage or implement retention policies.

data.title: CI/CD Capacity
data.text: CI/CD capacity directly affects developer productivity. If builds queue for more than 10 minutes, developers wait. Provision capacity proactively.
Capacity Planning and Cost Optimization

Capacity planning should balance performance and cost. Use reserved instances for baseline capacity and on-demand for spikes. Use spot instances for fault-tolerant batch workloads. Use auto-scaling to match capacity with demand. Right-size instances based on utilization data. Review capacity utilization monthly and right-size over-provisioned resources.

items: Use reserved instances for baseline capacity
Use spot instances for batch workloads
Right-size instances monthly based on utilization
Delete unused resources to reduce cost

data.text: Capacity Planning and Budgeting

Capacity planning should be part of the annual budgeting process. Project infrastructure costs based on traffic growth and capacity requirements. Include a contingency buffer for unexpected growth. Present the capacity plan to finance and leadership. Align infrastructure investment with business growth targets.

items: Project infrastructure costs based on traffic growth
Include contingency buffer for unexpected growth
Present capacity plan to finance and leadership
Align infrastructure investment with business targets

data.text: Capacity Planning and Procurement

Hardware procurement takes time. For on-premises or colocated infrastructure, order hardware three to six months before it is needed. For cloud infrastructure, capacity is available on demand but budget approval takes time. Plan procurement cycles to ensure capacity is available when needed.

items: On-premises: order 3 to 6 months before needed
Cloud: request budget approval 1 to 2 months before needed
Maintain a hardware buffer for emergency replacements
Use cloud for flexibility, on-premises for cost efficiency

data.text: Capacity Planning and Risk Management

Under-provisioning is a risk that causes incidents. Over-provisioning is a risk that wastes money. Balance these risks using the error budget framework. If the error budget is healthy, provision conservatively. If the error budget is low, provision aggressively and invest in reliability. Use capacity planning as a risk management tool.

data.title: Capacity Risk
data.text: Under-provisioning causes incidents. Over-provisioning wastes money. Use error budget to balance these risks.
Capacity Planning and Chaos Engineering

Chaos engineering validates capacity plans by simulating load and failure. Inject traffic spikes to verify that auto-scaling triggers correctly. Kill instances to verify that the system handles reduced capacity. Chaos experiments reveal capacity assumptions that are wrong and give you time to fix them before real traffic exposes the gap.

items: Inject traffic spikes to test auto-scaling
Kill instances to test degraded capacity handling
Verify the system remains within SLO under stress
Document findings and adjust capacity plan

data.text: Capacity Planning and Observability

Capacity planning depends on observability. You cannot plan for what you cannot measure. Deploy dashboards that show utilization trends, growth projections, and capacity warnings. Use anomaly detection to alert when utilization grows faster than expected. Make capacity data visible to the entire team.

items: Use anomaly detection for unexpected growth
Share capacity data with the engineering team

data.text: Capacity Planning and Incident Response

Capacity-related incidents require rapid response. The on-call engineer should have access to capacity dashboards and scaling controls. If the incident is caused by capacity, scale immediately and investigate the root cause later. Document the capacity incident in the postmortem and update the capacity plan to prevent recurrence.

data.title: Capacity Incident Response
data.content: When an incident is caused by capacity, scale first and investigate later. Document the incident and update the capacity plan.

data.text: Capacity Planning and Organizational Alignment

Capacity planning requires alignment between engineering, product, and finance. Engineering provides utilization data and capacity recommendations. Product provides traffic projections and launch schedules. Finance provides budget constraints. Meet quarterly to align on capacity needs and budget.

items: Engineering: provide utilization data and recommendations
Product: provide traffic projections and launch schedules
All three: meet quarterly to align on capacity needs

data.text: Capacity Planning and Documentation

Document the capacity plan in a shared wiki or runbook. Include the current utilization, growth projections, capacity limits, and scaling policies. Update the document quarterly. Make it accessible to on-call engineers so they can make informed decisions during incidents.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Capacity planning is proactive, not reactive.
Use auto-scaling to match capacity with demand.
Model traffic growth based on historical data and business plans.
Align capacity plans with engineering, product, and finance.
data.takeaway: Proactive capacity planning prevents incidents, reduces cost, and enables confident growth.

items.question: How much headroom should I provision?
items.answer: Provision 20 to 30 percent above projected peak. This absorbs traffic spikes and failed instances.

items.question: How often should I review capacity?
items.answer: Review quarterly for core services and before every major launch. Update the model after every significant traffic change.

items.question: What is the biggest capacity planning mistake?
items.answer: Using average utilization instead of peak utilization. Always plan for peak load.

items.question: How do I model seasonal traffic?
items.answer: Use historical data from previous seasonal periods. Provision two weeks before the event and scale down two weeks after.

items.question: How does capacity planning relate to SLOs?
items.answer: Insufficient capacity causes SLO breaches. Monitor utilization alongside error budget and scale before the budget is exhausted.
